result: The study addresses a fundamental knowledge gap in fish feeding: while external flows drawing food into the mouth are well-characterized, the mechanisms by which intraoral waterflows deposit food at the esophagus entrance remain unknown. This gap is significant because virtually all fishes rely on water flows for food transport, representing a fundamental aspect of feeding in more than half of all vertebrates.
evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C12-C22, C34-C35 collectively establish the background knowledge and identify the research gap. These claims are well-supported by multiple citations to established literature and accurately characterize the state of knowledge in the field. The identification of the knowledge gap is logical and well-justified.

result: The authors present a theoretical paradox: posteriorly moving water must curve laterally/ventrally to exit through gill slits, which would carry food away from the esophagus rather than toward it. This paradox necessitates a filtration mechanism to separate food from water streamlines, as the esophagus does not appear to directly draw water.
evaluation: Claims C4-C6, C23-C30 present a logical theoretical framework based on anatomical constraints and physical principles. The reasoning is sound and supported by citations to previous work (C23, C28). The paradox is well-articulated and provides clear motivation for the experimental investigation.

result: Three hypothetical intraoral flow patterns are proposed based on computational models and previous work on filter feeders: diverging flow, central jet, and branchial crossflow. These represent alternative mechanisms by which food could reach the pharyngeal jaws.
evaluation: Claims C31-C33 present well-founded hypotheses supported by computational modeling studies (C31) and work on filter feeders (C33). These hypotheses provide testable predictions for the experimental work. The citations are appropriate and the logic is sound.

result: The authors developed a novel technique combining biplanar high-speed X-ray videography (XROMM) with 3D X-ray particle tracking (XPT) of 1.4 mm neutrally buoyant spheres to simultaneously quantify intraoral waterflow patterns, food trajectories, and skeletal kinematics in vivo. The technique was applied to two carp and two tilapia individuals.
evaluation: Claims C7-C8, C36-C38, C83-C87, C133-C143 describe the methodological innovation. The technique is well-documented with appropriate technical specifications (750 fps, ±0.1 mm spatial resolution). The authors acknowledge limitations (small sample size, C134-C137) but justify the approach for qualitative pattern analysis. The method represents a genuine advance over previous invasive techniques (C85).

result: Water tracer particles were designed to be radio-opaque yet neutrally buoyant, consisting of 1.4 mm diameter EPS foam spheres pierced with 0.4 mm brass rods. The tracers had a mean density of 1031 ± 14 kg/m³ (N=11 used in experiments), representing a >5-fold volume reduction compared to previous X-ray particle tracking studies. Food pellets had a volume of 24 ± 2 mm³ and density of 1845 ± 170 kg/m³.
evaluation: Claims C144-C155 provide detailed characterization of the tracer particles with quantitative measurements. The design rationale is sound (C144, C147), manufacturing protocol is described (C145-C148), and density measurements are provided with appropriate sample sizes (C154-C155). The comparison to previous work (C149-C150) demonstrates the advance. The characterization is thorough and well-documented.

result: Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations validated that the 1.4 mm diameter particles with densities up to 1050 kg/m³ accurately track suction flows, with gravitational deviation <1 mm and acceptable lag/overshoot during acceleration/deceleration.
evaluation: Claims C156-C158 present CFD validation of the tracer particle performance. The simulations address a critical concern about whether the particles faithfully track water flow. The quantitative results (deviation <1 mm, acceptable lag/overshoot) support the use of these tracers for characterizing flow patterns. The validation is appropriate and strengthens confidence in the method.

result: Experimental data were collected using the 3D2YMOX biplanar X-ray system at 2048×2048 pixels and 750 fps. From 73 recorded sequences, 13 successful trials were selected for analysis. Post-experiment μCT scans were used to reconstruct bone models and marker positions.
evaluation: Claims C159-C166 describe the data collection and processing workflow. The technical specifications are appropriate and well-documented. The selection criteria for successful trials (C164) are reasonable. The workflow from video acquisition through 3D reconstruction is standard for XROMM studies and properly executed.

result: Water tracers exhibited stereotypical bidirectional motion patterns during feeding: an initial slow approach (3.9±2.5 cm/s in carp, 3.3±1.3 cm/s in tilapia), followed by rapid intake (reaching 92.1±59 cm/s in carp, 97.8±23 cm/s in tilapia over 0.26-0.27 s), then alternating reverse flows and backflows with consistent periodicity (0.58±0.12 s in carp, 0.40±0.05 s in tilapia).
evaluation: Claims C39-C53 present quantitative kinematic data from the experiments (carp: 2 individuals, 7 trials; tilapia: 2 individuals, 6 trials). The patterns were consistent across trials (C50) and automatically detectable (C50), indicating robust phenomena. The quantitative measurements are well-documented with means and standard deviations. The temporal patterns are clearly characterized.

result: No water tracers passed through the esophagus in any of the 73 trials, while food was successfully ingested in most cases (29/34 carp trials, 30/36 tilapia trials). Food tracers traveled significantly shorter distances than water tracers, demonstrating different trajectories.
evaluation: Claims C54-C57 present a key finding with clear quantitative data across a large number of trials. The complete separation of water and food trajectories (C54) is striking and well-documented. The statistical comparison of distances (C56) with appropriate analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) supports the conclusion of different paths (C57). This is strong evidence for food-water separation.

result: During intake, food followed a more dorsal trajectory close to the midsagittal plane, while water tracers spread throughout the buccal cavity with only 3-5 per trial following midsagittal trajectories. Path curvature was significantly higher for water tracers than food tracers in both species, indicating greater lateral deviation of water.
evaluation: Claims C58-C64 describe spatial separation of food and water trajectories with both qualitative observations (C58-C62) and quantitative statistical analysis (C63-C64). The significant difference in path curvature (C63, Figure 4) provides strong evidence for differential trajectories. The finding that tilapia showed earlier deviation (C62) suggests species differences. The evidence is compelling and well-presented.

result: Tilapia exhibited a prominent central jet flow pattern with anterior flow near buccal cavity borders, while carp showed this pattern only near the mouth entrance with diverging flow posteriorly. No clear posteriomedial flows indicative of branchial crossflow were observed in either species.
evaluation: Claims C65-C71 characterize species-specific flow patterns. The identification of central jet in tilapia (C65-C66) and its limited presence in carp (C67-C68) is supported by the trajectory data (Figure 4). The negative finding regarding crossflow (C69-C71) is clearly stated. The species differences are well-documented, though the mechanistic basis requires further study (acknowledged in C103).

result: No significant correlation was found between ingestion timing and final particle location in the buccal cavity (Kendall test: carp p=0.27, tilapia p=0.21). However, qualitative observations suggest early-ingested particles tend to remain medial while late ones move lateral. Particles generally stay on the same side but can switch, with significant correlation between initial and final lateromedial position in carp (p=0.000287) but not tilapia (p=0.08).
evaluation: Claims C72-C75 present statistical analyses of particle trajectories. The lack of correlation between timing and anteroposterior position (C72) is clearly stated with p-values. The qualitative observation (C73) is appropriately hedged. The species difference in lateromedial correlation (C75) is interesting and statistically supported. The mixed quantitative/qualitative findings are appropriately presented.

result: Skeletal kinematics revealed stereotypical sequences: during intake, peak gape was followed by peak hyoid depression, then peak opercula abduction. During reverse flow, this sequence was inverted. During backflow, the same sequence as intake occurred but with lower magnitudes. These patterns were consistent across all trials in both species.
evaluation: Claims C76-C82 describe kinematic patterns from 3D motion analysis (carp: 2 individuals, 7 trials; tilapia: 1 individual, 3 trials). The stereotypical sequences (C77, C81) and their consistency (C78, C82) are clearly documented. The link between opercula abduction and lateral water motion (C79) connects skeletal motion to flow patterns. The reduced sample size for tilapia kinematics is a limitation but the consistency across trials supports the findings.

result: The particle manufacturing protocol could be further optimized to reduce density variability, potentially enabling tracking of flows with weaker pressure gradients. Miniaturization of mold-based manufacturing for 8 mm particles might be possible. The X-ray particle tracking method has strong potential as a tool for studying water motion in optically inaccessible systems.
evaluation: Claims C88-C91 are speculations about future improvements and applications. While reasonable, these are not findings from the current study. The potential for optimization (C88-C89) and miniaturization (C90) are plausible but undemonstrated. The broader potential (C91) is a reasonable extrapolation but remains to be validated in other systems.

result: The study addresses how food reaches the esophagus when water flows toward gill slits. Both species positioned food close to midsagittal streamlines, with direct pharyngeal jaw interception being common. The authors hypothesize two mechanisms: (1) central jet flow pattern and (2) inertial effects from food size/density. Evidence supports the central jet mechanism, which was previously observed in computational models but dismissed as artifact.
evaluation: Claims C92-C100 present the central findings and interpretation. The observation that fish successfully position food medially (C94-C95) is well-documented. The two-mechanism hypothesis (C96) is reasonable and supported by the data. The validation of central jet patterns from CFD models (C97-C100) is significant, as it confirms that a previously dismissed computational result is biologically real. The evidence is strong.

result: CFD models indicate diverging flow gradually transitions to central jet during suction, which would increase food interception probability near the esophagus and enhance suction efficiency. The mechanistic basis for the more prominent central jet in tilapia versus carp requires further research and likely relates to differences in mouth shape, buccal cavity shape, or expansion kinematics.
evaluation: Claims C101-C103 integrate computational modeling with experimental observations. The CFD results (C101) provide mechanistic insight into flow pattern development. The functional interpretation (C102) is logical. The acknowledgment that species differences require further study (C103) is appropriate and honest about the limits of current understanding.

result: Significantly higher path curvature for water versus food tracers indicates inertial effects separate food from water flow. While intuitive for large prey, the data suggest this inertia-driven filtration mechanism is effective even for relatively small pellets and operates at the full scale of the buccopharyngeal cavity, not just at branchial arches as previously hypothesized for filter feeders.
evaluation: Claims C104-C109 present the inertial separation mechanism with statistical support (C104, Figure 4). The extension from large to small prey (C105-C106) is an important finding. The connection to crossflow filtration in filter feeders (C107) provides context, while demonstrating this operates at larger scale (C108) is novel. The acknowledgment that food properties need further quantification (C109) is appropriate.

result: Flow patterns matching branchial crossflow were not identified. The authors speculate this may be because the food type offered did not require such filtration.
evaluation: Claims C110-C111 present a negative finding with appropriate speculation about the reason. The absence of crossflow (C110) is clearly stated. The speculation (C111) is reasonable but unproven. This is an honest reporting of what was not observed, with appropriate caution about interpretation.

result: After initial capture, omnivorous species perform food sorting and processing via periodical back-and-forth water motions. These reverse flows (previously termed 'back-wash') move food anteriorly toward the palatal organ in carp, where edible particles are clamped while waste is flushed through gill slits. These flows are important for food sorting and potentially prevent gill slit clogging, likely involving gill slits functioning as flow inlets.
evaluation: Claims C112-C118 integrate current observations with previous work on food processing. The back-and-forth motions (C113) are well-documented in the current study. The connection to previous observations of reverse flows (C114) and the palatal organ hypothesis (C115) is appropriate. The functional interpretations (C116-C117) are logical. The inference about gill slits as inlets (C118) is reasonable and supported by citation.

result: The study provides first empirical evidence of bidirectional waterflows synchronized with jaw, hyoid, and opercula motions creating anterior-to-posterior waves during backflows and posterior-to-anterior waves during reverse flows. The classical anterior-to-posterior wave was observed during backflows, but waterflow was also guided ventrally by hyoid depression and laterally by opercula abduction. No particles entered the esophagus during backward water motion, confirming no water enters the esophagus. These alternations eventually position food centrally near pharyngeal jaws.
evaluation: Claims C119-C126 present novel findings linking skeletal kinematics to flow patterns. The synchronization of bidirectional flows with skeletal motions (C119) is a first empirical demonstration. The observations of classical patterns (C122) with additional complexity (C123) add nuance. The confirmation that no water enters the esophagus (C124) is important. The functional outcome (C126) integrates the observations. This is strong, novel evidence.

result: The study highlights the biomechanical complexity of intraoral feeding processes, showing how high-velocity suction flow patterns affect food deposit sites and how centralized streams direct food toward the esophagus. Omnivorous species follow intake with repeated hydrodynamically driven repositioning for food sorting. Future research could reveal variation across feeding modes, morphologies, and sizes.
evaluation: Claims C127-C130 provide appropriate summary of the main findings. The complexity (C127), flow pattern effects (C128), central jet function (C129), and repositioning behavior (C130) are all well-supported by the data. The suggestions for future research (C131-C132) are reasonable extrapolations. This is an appropriate synthesis of the work.
